concept.name: Block bootstrap
concept.definition: A bootstrap variant for dependent data that resamples contiguous blocks of observations rather than individual points, preserving short-run serial dependence within each block while still generating artificial samples. Developed by Kunsch (1989) as the moving-blocks bootstrap.
concept.intuition: Resampling single returns would shuffle away the volatility clustering and momentum you need to preserve, so you resample whole chunks of consecutive days and let dependence live inside each chunk.
concept.mechanics: Divide the series into overlapping (moving-blocks) or non-overlapping blocks of length l, resample the blocks with replacement, concatenate them into pseudo-series of length n, and recompute the statistic on each. Block length trades bias (too short breaks dependence) against variance (too long leaves few distinct blocks), with l typically growing as n^{1/3}.
concept.formula: For x_1,...,x_n, blocks B_i = (x_i, ..., x_{i+l-1}); a bootstrap sample concatenates ceiling(n/l) blocks drawn uniformly with replacement.
concept.failure_modes: Results are sensitive to block length, and dependence spanning more than the block length is still severed at block boundaries, biasing statistics that depend on long memory.
concept.misconceptions: That any block length works once blocks are used: too-short blocks reproduce the i.i.d. bootstrap's failure on dependent data, and the choice is a genuine tuning problem.
concept.example: Testing a trend-following rule's t-statistic: generate moving-block bootstrap return series with l = 20 days, rerun the rule on each, and compare the real t-statistic to the bootstrap distribution.
